titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §153–169: crimes in the family, betrothal gifts, dowries and disinheritance (xxv 61 – xxviii 37)
part: Laws §153–169 · family crimes, betrothal gifts & disinheritance (Col. xxv 61 – xxviii 37)
about: Seventeen laws about the family under strain. A wife who has her husband killed for another man is put on a stake (§153); then four laws on sex inside the family, all stated without softening: a father and his daughter, who is driven from the city (§154); a father and the bride chosen for his son, who is drowned if he lies with her after his son has known her, but only fined if the son had not (§155–156); a son and his mother, both burned (§157); a son caught in the lap of his father’s chief wife is cast out of his father’s house (§158). Next come the gifts that pass at a betrothal: if the groom changes his mind he loses what he brought; if the bride’s father changes his, he pays it back double; and a rival who slandered the groom does not get the girl (§159–161). Then what happens to a dead wife’s dowry (§162–164), how brothers share their father’s estate when he has favoured one son or married off all but the youngest (§165–166), and when a man had children by two wives (§167). The last two laws let a father disown his son, but only after the judges have examined the case, and only for a second grave offence (§168–169). Harper’s transliteration writes the Sumerian signs for ‘child’, ‘woman’, ‘house’, ‘silver’ and ‘bride’ as Akkadian words, and each was read from the plate; the few doubtful spellings are marked in the notes.

sentences.l: If the-wife of-a-man on-account-of another male her-husband has-had-killed, woman that on-a-stake they-shall-set-her.
sentences.i: If a man’s wife has had her husband killed on account of another man, they shall put that woman on a stake.
sentences.n: A new law, and its verb is a causative. mussa ušdīk is “she has had her husband killed”: mussa (written mu-za) is mut “husband of” + -ša “her”, the t and š merged into ss as in §141–152, and ušdīk is the Š-stem of dâkum “to kill”. The Š-stem is the causative, marked by the š before the root (u-š-dīk), so “kill” becomes “cause to be killed”; Harper’s glossary lists it as the third stem of dâkum. aššum zikārim šanîm is “on account of another male”, the words of §132: aššum “because of” takes the genitive. The penalty is zinništam šuāti ina gašīšim išakkanūši, “that woman they shall set on a stake”: gašīšum is a stake or pole (Harper: “stake, pole”), and to set a person on one is to impale her; the text says no more than the words. zinništam is the sign SAL alone, išakkanū the plural present of šakānum “to set”, -ši “her”.

sentences.l: If a-man his-daughter has-known, man that the-city they-shall-make-leave-him.
sentences.i: If a man has had intercourse with his daughter, they shall drive that man out of the city.
sentences.n: Incest with a daughter, stated without softening. mārassu is “his daughter”: DUMU “child” and SAL “woman”, then ZU for -ssu; the t of mārat and the š of -šu merge into ss, the same assimilation as in mussa. iltamad is the perfect of lamādum “to learn, to know”, and in this code “to know” a person is to have sex with her or him (Harper’s glossary: “know carnally”); the same verb returns in §155–156. awīlam šuāti is “that man”. ālam “the city” is one sign, URU (Harper prints alam). ušeṣṣûšu is the Š-stem of waṣûm “to go out”, present plural, + -šu “him”: “they shall make him go out”. Harper prints u-še-iz-zu-u-šu, writing ṣ as z; the signs are IṢ and ZU, and the doubled ṣṣ they spell is what marks the present (the preterite would be ušēṣû). The penalty is banishment.

sentences.l: If a-man for his-son a-bride has-chosen-and, his-son has-known-her,
sentences.i: If a man has chosen a bride for his son, and his son has had intercourse with her,
sentences.n: A law about three people: a father, his son, and the bride the father has arranged for the son. The first clause is awīlum … iḫīrma, “a man has chosen (a bride) …”: iḫīr is the preterite of ḫiārum “to choose” (Harper: “to betroth”; the verb behind ḫīrtum “wife”), here “has chosen (a bride)”, with -ma “and”. ana mārišu “for his son” is ana + the genitive. kallātam “bride” is a Sumerogram, É.GI₄.A: the sign for house, the sign GI₄ and the sign A, three signs in all and no ending written (Harper’s glossary gives the same logogram, E.GE.A, and his List of Signs shows kallâtu as these three signs; his transliteration adds the case ending, kal-lâtam). The plate shows this spelling twice, at XXV 74 and XXVI 4. māršu ilmassi is “his son has known her”: lamādum “to know” (see §154) in the preterite, with -ši “her”; the d of ilmad and the š of -ši merge into ss, and the sign ZI writes the ssi.

sentences.l: he afterwards in her-lap has-lain-and they-have-seized-him, man that they-shall-bind-him-and into the-water they-shall-throw-(him).
sentences.i: and he afterwards has lain in her lap and they have caught him, they shall bind that man and throw him into the water.
sentences.n: The father is caught. šū warkānumma is “he afterwards” (warkānum “afterwards” + -ma). ina sūniša ittatīlma iṣṣabtūšu, “he has lain in her lap and they have seized him”, is the clause of §130 word for word: sūnum “lap”, ittatīl the perfect of itūlum “to lie”, iṣṣabtūšu the perfect plural of ṣabātum “to seize” (the t of the perfect is taken into the ṣ) with -šu “him”. Then the formula of §129: ikassûšuma (kasûm “to bind” + -šu + -ma) and ana mê inaddûši, “into the water they shall throw (him)”; nadûm is “to throw”. UNCERTAIN: the last word ends in -ši, which elsewhere is “her”, though the man is the object; the plate shows the sign ši there, and I translate “him” as the sense requires. The verdict is drowning, stated as plainly as every other penalty.

sentences.l: If a-man for his-son a-bride has-chosen-and, his-son not has-known-her-and, he in her-lap has-lain,
sentences.i: If a man has chosen a bride for his son, and his son has not had intercourse with her, and he himself has lain in her lap,
sentences.n: The same opening as §155 with one difference: the son has not known the bride. mār-šu lā ilmassima is “his son has not known her, and” (lā “not”, -ma “and”). šū is “he”, the father, standing alone for emphasis; ina sūniša ittatīl is “in her lap he has lain”, the perfect without -ma. The condition is complete here; the penalty, which is a fine and not death, follows in the next unit.

sentences.l: half a-mina of-silver he-shall-pay-her-and, and anything which from the-house of-her-father she-brought he-shall-make-good-to-her-and, the-husband of-her-heart shall-take-her.
sentences.i: he shall pay her half a mina of silver, and he shall make good to her whatever she brought from her father’s house, and the husband of her heart (the man she likes) shall take her as wife.
sentences.n: A fine, restitution and release. mišil mana kaspim is “half a mina of silver”: ½ has a sign of its own, ma-na is spelled in syllables (as at §59), and kaspim is the two signs KÙ.BABBAR with the ending -im; the plate line is crowded and I could not match every stroke group to a sign, so the six signs follow Harper’s ½ ma-na kaspim, UNCERTAIN. išaqqalšimma is “he shall pay her” (šaqālum “to weigh out, to pay”, -šim “to her”, -ma “and”). u mimma ša ištu bīt abiša ublam is “and anything that she brought from her father’s house”: her dowry, as in §138; ušallamšimma is the D-stem of šalāmum “to make whole”, “he shall make good to her”. Last, mut libbiša iḫḫazzi, as in §137: mut “husband of” (written mu-tu) + libbiša “her heart”, so “the husband of her heart”, the man she herself wants; iḫḫazzi is iḫḫaz “he shall take (as wife)” + -ši “her”, the z and š merged.

sentences.l: If a-man after his-father in the-lap of-his-mother has-lain, both-of-them they-shall-burn-them.
sentences.i: If a man, after his father’s death, has lain in his mother’s lap, they shall burn them both.
sentences.n: Incest with the mother. warki abišu is literally “after his father”; the sense “after his father’s death” comes from the context, and the next law uses the same words. ina sūn ummišu is “in the lap of his mother”: sūn is sūnum in the construct state (written zu-un), ummišu is ummum “mother” + -šu; ittatīl as in §155. The penalty names both: kilallīšunu “both of them” (kilallān + -šunu; Harper writes ki-la-li, with li, here and ki-la-la at §152, and the sense is the same) and iqallûšunūti “they shall burn them”, the present plural of qalûm “to burn” with -šunūti “them”. The text says only “burn”, and so do I.

sentences.l: If a-man after his-father in the-lap of-his-senior-one who children has-borne has-been-seized, man that from the-house of-the-father he-shall-be-uprooted.
sentences.i: If a man, after his father’s death, is caught in the lap of his father’s chief wife (?), who has borne children, that man shall be cast out of his father’s house.
sentences.n: Not the man’s mother this time but another woman of the house. rabītišu is rabûm “great, senior” in the feminine + -šu “his”, literally “his senior one”; I read “his” as the father’s and the woman as the father’s principal wife (Harper: “chief wife”), UNCERTAIN, because the word itself says neither whose she is nor that she is a wife. ša mārī waldat is “who has borne children” (mārī, DUMU with the plural signs; waldat the stative “she has borne”). ittaṣbat “he was caught” is the N-stem perfect, the passive, as in §129. The penalty is lighter than in §157: innassaḫ is the N-stem of nasāḫum “to pull out, to uproot”, “he shall be uprooted”, here cast out of the family house (Harper: “cut off”); the same verb carries §168–169. bīt abim “his father’s house” is written bît a-ba, where Harper’s a-ba stands for the genitive abim; the spelling is Harper’s, UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: If a-man who to the-house of-his-father-in-law a-present has-had-brought, a-bride-price has-given,
sentences.i: If a man who has had a present brought to his father-in-law’s house, and has given the bride-price,
sentences.n: The first of three laws about betrothal gifts; the first is the groom’s change of mind. The long “if” is built on a ša-relative clause: awīlum ša … ušābilu … iddinu, “a man who had (a present) brought … gave”; ša “who” makes both verbs end in -u, the subjunctive. bīt emišu is “the house of his father-in-law” (emum “father-in-law”). biblam is biblum “what is brought, a present” (Harper), the gift sent with the betrothal, which is separate from the tirḫatum “bride-price”. ušābilu is the Š-stem of wabālum “to carry”, so “had carried”: the groom does not carry it himself. iddinu is nadānum “to give”.

sentences.l: to a-woman another he-has-looked-with-longing (?), and to his-father-in-law “your-daughter not I-will-take” he-has-said,
sentences.i: has looked longingly (?) at another woman, and has said to his father-in-law, “I will not take your daughter,”
sentences.n: The groom turns away. uptallisma is the perfect of the D-stem of palāsum, which Harper glosses “to look with longing” (the perfect puts -ta- after the first consonant: up-ta-llis); “look longingly” is his sense, UNCERTAIN because the verb is rare. ana zinništim šanītim is “at another woman”, zinništim being the sign SAL alone, with no ending written (the plate shows none between SAL and the next word). mārtaka ul aḫḫaz is the quoted refusal: mārtaka “your daughter” (DUMU.SAL and ka), ul aḫḫaz “I shall not take” (spelled a-ḫa-az, the doubling not written), the first person of the present of aḫāzum, so a firm “I will not”. iqtabi “he has said” closes the quotation, as in §141–142.

sentences.l: the-father of-the-daughter whatever which was-brought-to-him he-shall-take-away.
sentences.i: the father of the daughter shall take away whatever was brought to him.
sentences.n: The groom who breaks it off loses what he sent. abī mārtim is “the father of the daughter”: abī is abum in the construct state, mārtim the genitive (DUMU.SAL, the signs for “child” and “woman”, with no ending written). mimma ša ibbablušum is “anything that was brought to him”: ibbablu is wabālum in the N-stem (preterite), so “was carried”, with -šum “to him”; the -u is the subjunctive of the ša-clause, short before -šum as in innadnušum (§112–126); Harper’s glossary lists it as the passive (IV, 1) of “to bring”. itabbal is the present of tabālum “to carry off”, “he shall take away”; the father keeps it.

sentences.l: If a-man to the-house of-father-in-law a-present has-had-brought, a-bride-price he-has-given-and,
sentences.i: If a man has had a present brought to his father-in-law’s house and has given the bride-price,
sentences.n: The same facts as §159, now with the refusal coming from the other side. This unit is the condition only: ana bīt emim “to the house of the father-in-law” (emim, the genitive), ušābil “he has had brought” (the Š-stem preterite, with no -u because there is no ša here), iddinma “he has given, and”.

sentences.l: the-father of-the-daughter “my-daughter not I-will-give-you” has-said,
sentences.i: and the father of the daughter has said, “I will not give you my daughter,”
sentences.n: It is the bride’s father who now breaks the match. mārtī ul anaddikkum is the quotation: mārtī “my daughter” (DUMU.SAL, and i for -ī “my”); ul anaddikkum “I shall not give (her) to you”: anaddin is the first person present of nadānum “to give”, and the n merges into the k of -kum “to you”. iqtabi “he has said” closes it.

sentences.l: anything as-much-as was-brought-to-him he-shall-double-and he-shall-return.
sentences.i: he shall double everything that was brought to him and return it.
sentences.n: The father who withdraws pays back twice what came. mimma mala ibbablušum is “anything, as much as was brought to him” (mala “as much as”, as in §106). uštašannâma is Harper’s šanûm “to repeat, to do again” in the Š-stem with -ma, read “he shall double (it)”: the form is UNCERTAIN (ušta- with a doubled n could be a Š perfect or a Št present) and the sense follows the penalty. utâr is the present of the D-stem of târum, “he shall give back”. Harper prints a dot under the t of u-ṭa-ar here and none in the same word at XXVI 74; on the plate the sign is TA in both places, so I read ta, and the dot is the printed page’s.

sentences.l: If a-man to the-house of-his-father-in-law a-present has-had-brought, a-bride-price he-has-given-and, his-friend has-slandered-him,
sentences.i: If a man has had a present brought to his father-in-law’s house, and has given the bride-price, and his friend has slandered him,
sentences.n: §161 adds a third person to §159–160. The groom has sent his present and paid the bride-price, and a friend now spoils it. ibiršu is ibrum “friend, companion” + -šu “his”. uktarriṣṣu (written ug-dar-ri-zu) is the perfect of the D-stem of karāṣum, Harper’s “to slander”, with -šu “him”; the ṣ and š merge into ṣṣ, spelled with the sign ZU, and the first sign is UG, Harper’s ug (List of Signs no. 62, the sign for ug/uk/uq; not the IG of iqtabi) (the perfect puts -ta- after the first consonant: uk-tar-riṣ). The verb is rare and the form UNCERTAIN, but “slandered him” is what the story needs, and it is Harper’s sense.

sentences.l: his-father-in-law to the-owner of-the-wife “my-daughter not you-will-take” has-said,
sentences.i: and his father-in-law has said to the man entitled to the wife, “You shall not take my daughter,”
sentences.n: emušu is “his father-in-law”, the subject. bēl aššatim is literally “the owner of the wife”: the man who holds the claim to the woman, that is, the groom who paid (Harper: “the claimant for the wife”); “entitled to the wife” is my reading of the phrase, and bēl is spelled be-el, not with the sign EN. mārtī ul taḫḫaz is the quotation: ul taḫḫaz “you shall not take”, the second person of the present of aḫāzum.

sentences.l: anything as-much-as was-brought-to-him he-shall-double-and he-shall-return,
sentences.i: he shall double everything that was brought to him and return it,
sentences.n: The same words as the penalty in §160 (mimma mala ibbablušum uštašannâma utâr), now spoken of the father-in-law who has sent the groom away on the strength of the slander. The ruling about the slanderer follows.

sentences.l: and his-wife his-friend not he-shall-take.
sentences.i: and his friend shall not take his wife.
sentences.n: The slanderer gains nothing. aššassu is “his wife” (aš-ša-zu: aššat + -šu, the t and š merged into ss and written with ZU, as in mussa): the bride is called the groom’s wife already, because the bride-price has been paid. ibiršu ul iḫḫaz is “his friend shall not take”: the third person present of aḫāzum, where §161 above had the second person taḫḫaz.

sentences.l: If a-man a-wife has-taken-and children she-bore-to-him, woman that to fate has-gone,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife and she has borne him children, and that woman has gone to her fate,
sentences.n: Three laws on the dowry (šeriqtum) of a wife who dies. aššatam iḫuz is “he has taken a wife” (iḫuz, the preterite of aḫāzum “to take”; the code’s usual way to say “married”). mārī ūlissumma is “children she bore him, and” (-ma “and”): ūlissum is ūlid “she bore” + -šum “to him”, the d and š merged into ss, and the last syllable is one complex sign, which Harper reads zum; his List of Signs has no entry for it, so the identification is UNCERTAIN (the same sign stands at XXVII 77). mārī is DUMU with the plural signs. ana šīmtim ittalak “she has gone to her fate” is the code’s phrase for dying, as in §12.

sentences.l: to her-dowry her-father not he-shall-claim; her-dowry (is) of-her-children alone.
sentences.i: her father shall not lay claim to her dowry; her dowry belongs to her children alone.
sentences.n: When the wife leaves children, her dowry goes to them, not back to her father. abūša is “her father” (abum + -ša). ana šeriqtiša ul iraggum is “he shall not claim her dowry”: ragāmum “to claim, to raise a claim”, iraggum the present with the ventive ending -m (the claim he would make for himself). šeriqtaša ša mārīšama is “her dowry is her children’s”: ša “of” + mārīša “her children” + -ma, which singles them out, “and no one else’s”.

sentences.l: If a-man a-wife has-taken-and children not she-made-him-acquire, woman that to fate has-gone,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife and she has not given him children, and that woman has gone to her fate,
sentences.n: The opposite case: no children. mārī lā ušaršišu is “she did not make him acquire children”: ušaršišu is rašûm “to acquire” in the Š-stem (“to make acquire”) with -šu “him”, the same stem as ušaršušu in §137; the subject is the wife. zinništum šī is “that woman”, zinništum written with the sign SAL alone, šī “she, that”.

sentences.l: If the-bride-price which that man to the-house of-his-father-in-law brought, his-father-in-law has-returned-to-him,
sentences.i: if his father-in-law has returned to him the bride-price that that man brought to his father-in-law’s house,
sentences.n: A second “if” inside the same law: the answer depends on whether the bride-price was given back. tirḫatam ša awīlum šū ana bīt emišu ublu is “the bride-price that that man brought to his father-in-law’s house” (ublu, the subjunctive after ša). uttēršum is the perfect of the D-stem of târum “to return” with -šum “to him”: “has returned to him”.

sentences.l: to the-dowry of-woman that her-husband not he-shall-claim; her-dowry of-the-house of-her-father (is) alone.
sentences.i: her husband shall not lay claim to that woman’s dowry; her dowry belongs to her father’s house alone.
sentences.n: Compare §162: there it was the father who could not claim, here it is the husband. Harper prints zin-ništim, with a hyphen; on the plate it is the single sign SAL, followed by šu-a-ti (XXVII 20). mussa ul iraggum is “her husband shall not claim”; Harper prints a dot under the g of i-ra-ag̣-gu-um, which I take for dirt, as the word at XXVII 4 has none. šeriqtaša ša bīt abiša-ma is “her dowry (is) of her father’s house, alone”, with -ma as in §162.

sentences.l: If his-father-in-law the-bride-price not has-returned-to-him,
sentences.i: If his father-in-law has not returned the bride-price to him,
sentences.n: The case of the withheld bride-price. lā uttēršum is the verb of §163 with lā “not”: “he has not returned to him”.

sentences.l: from her-dowry as-much-as her-bride-price he-shall-deduct-and her-dowry to the-house of-her-father he-shall-return.
sentences.i: he shall deduct from her dowry as much as her bride-price, and return her dowry to her father’s house.
sentences.n: The husband takes back his bride-price out of the dowry and returns the rest. iḫarraṣma is the present of ḫarāṣum “to cut off, to deduct” (Harper: “to deduct”) with -ma; mala tirḫatiša “as much as her bride-price”. utâr is the D-stem present of târum, “he shall return”. At XXVII 31 the stone has a carver’s slip, which Harper notes as a-ta(=bi)-ša: the sign is TA where BI is needed, and the word is abiša “her father’s”.

sentences.l: If a-man to his-son who his-eye (is) first a-field, an-orchard and a-house has-given, a-sealed-document he-wrote-for-him,
sentences.i: If a man has given a field, an orchard and a house to the son he favours (?), and has written him a sealed document,
sentences.n: A father’s gift to one son. ana mārišu ša īnšu maḫru is “to his son, whose eye is maḫru”: īnšu is īnum “eye” + -šu, and maḫru is the adjective “first, foremost” or a stative of maḫārum “to face”; the idiom is read as “the son he favours” (Harper: “favorite son”), UNCERTAIN. The gift is three Sumerograms: eqlam is A.ŠÀ, kirâm is {giš}KIRI₆, bītam is É, “a field, an orchard and a house”. išruk “he has given (as a gift)” is šarākum; Harper prints the last sign as uq in his text and uk in his glossary, and the sign UG (his List no. 62) reads either. kunukkam išṭuršum is “a sealed document he wrote for him”: kunukkum “sealed tablet”, šaṭārum “to write”, -šum “to him”; Harper’s kunukkam is written here ku-nu-kam, the last sign being the KAM sign (his List no. 157, kam/gam), as in the earlier laws. Two spots on the plate are UNCERTAIN: the ṭur of išṭuršum is drawn as a diamond with an inner triangle, not as the box-and-wedges DUMU sign (compare Harper’s List no. 53, dur), so the TUR glyph shown is only the nearest sign in the glossary; and at XXVII 34 a small extra sign stands between DUMU and ŠU that Harper’s mâri-šu does not record (a sign, or a flaw in the stone).

sentences.l: After the-father to fate has-gone, when the-brothers divide, the-gift which the-father gave-him he-shall-take-and,
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate, when the brothers divide the estate, he shall take the gift that the father gave him, and
sentences.n: warka abum ana šīmtim ittalku is “after the father has gone to his fate”: warka “after”, ittalku the verb with the subjunctive -u. inūma aḫḫū izuzzū is “when the brothers divide”: aḫḫū “brothers” (the plural of aḫum), izuzzū the present plural of zâzum “to divide”. qīšti abum iddinušum is “the gift that the father gave him”: qīštum “gift”, iddinu “he gave” with the -u of the relative clause, -šum “to him”. ileqqēma is the present of leqûm “to take” with -ma: “he shall take, and”.

sentences.l: in-addition from the-property of-the-house of-the-father equally they-shall-divide.
sentences.i: and in addition they shall divide the property of the father’s house equally.
sentences.n: elēnumma is “in addition, over and above”, as in §57; here it marks that the favoured son’s gift does not come out of the shared estate. ŠA-GA is the Sumerogram for makkūrum “property”, the signs GAR and GA (modern books write NÍG.GA; Harper reads the first sign ŠA); he prints a hyphen here and a period at XXVII 63, and the plate shows the same two signs. ina makkūr bīt abim is “from the property of the father’s house”; bīt abim is written bît a-ba (see §158). mitḫāriš izuzzū “they shall divide equally”.

sentences.l: If a-man for the-sons whom he-acquired wives has-taken, for his-son the-young a-wife not he-has-taken,
sentences.i: If a man has taken wives for the sons he has acquired, but has not taken a wife for his young son,
sentences.n: A father marries off his elder sons and dies before the youngest is married. ana mārī ša iršû aššātim iḫuz is “for the sons whom he has acquired he took wives”: ša iršû “whom he has acquired” (rašûm “to get”, with the -u after ša); aššātim is the plural “wives”, though the signs aš-ša-tim could also spell the singular aššatim; the plural suits ana mārī “for the sons”. ṣiḫrim is ṣeḫrum “small, young”, agreeing with mārišu “his son”; lā iḫuz “he has not taken”.

sentences.l: after the-father to fate has-gone, when the-brothers divide, from the-property of-the-house of-the-father
sentences.i: after the father has gone to his fate, when the brothers divide, from the property of the father’s house
sentences.n: The same frame as §165 (warka abum ana šīmtim ittalku, inūma aḫḫū izuzzū, ina makkūr bīt abim), now with ŠA.GA written with a period (the plate has the same two signs, GAR and GA). The sentence goes on into the next unit.

sentences.l: to their-brother the-young who a-wife not they-have-taken, in-addition-to his-share, silver of-the-bride-price
sentences.i: to their young brother, who has not taken a wife, in addition to his share, silver for a bride-price
sentences.n: ana aḫīšunu ṣiḫrim is “to their young brother” (aḫīšunu: aḫum “brother” + -šunu “their”). ša aššatam lā iḫzu is “who has not taken a wife”: iḫzu is iḫuz with the -u of the relative clause, the middle vowel dropped. eliāt zittišu is “over and above his share” (eliāt “beyond”, zittum “share”). kasap tirḫatim is “silver of the bride-price”: kasap is the construct state of kaspum (Harper prints kaspi), written with KÙ.BABBAR and no ending sign; on the plate the line is KÙ, BABBAR, TIR, ḪA, TIM, with nothing after BABBAR.

sentences.l: they-shall-set-for-him-and, a-wife they-shall-make-him-take.
sentences.i: they shall set it aside for him, and they shall have him take a wife.
sentences.n: The brothers pay for the marriage. išakkanūšumma is šakānum “to set” in the plural present with -šum “for him” and -ma. ušaḫḫazūšu is aḫāzum “to take” in the Š-stem, “to make take”, with -šu “him”: “they shall have him take a wife”. The Š-stem is the causative that opened this part at §153.

sentences.l: If a-man a-wife has-taken-and children she-bore-to-him, woman that to fate has-gone,
sentences.i: If a man has taken a wife and she has borne him children, and that woman has gone to her fate,
sentences.n: A man who marries twice and has children by both wives. The first marriage is the condition of §162 in the same words (aššatam iḫuz … mārī ūlissum … ana šīmtim ittalak); only the placing of -ma differs, iḫuzma here and ūlissumma there.

sentences.l: after-her a-woman another he-has-taken-and children she-has-borne,
sentences.i: and after her he has taken another woman, and she has borne children,
sentences.n: warkīša “after her” is warki “after” + -ša “her”. itaḫaz is the perfect of aḫāzum “to take”, “he has taken”, and ittalad the perfect of walādum “to bear”, “she has borne”; both are the perfect, the tense of the completed event, as ittalak was in the first clause.

sentences.l: afterwards the-father to fate has-gone: the-sons by-mothers not they-shall-divide,
sentences.i: and afterwards the father has gone to his fate: the sons shall not divide by mothers,
sentences.n: warkānum abum ana šīmtim ittalku “afterwards the father has gone to his fate”: ittalku has the -u of a clause that depends on the next one. mārū ana ummātim ul izuzzū is “the sons shall not divide by mothers”: ummātim is the plural of ummum “mother” (Harper’s glossary lists this form) and ana “according to”; the sense, fixed by the next unit, is that the sons do not divide the estate mother by mother. mārū is DUMU with the plural signs, here the subject.

sentences.l: the-dowry of-their-mothers they-shall-take-and, the-property of-the-house of-the-father equally they-shall-divide.
sentences.i: they shall take the dowries of their mothers, and the property of their father’s house they shall divide equally.
sentences.n: Each woman’s dowry goes to her own sons; the rest is shared in equal parts. šeriqti ummātišunu is “the dowry of their mothers”, šeriqti the construct state. ileqqûma is the present plural of leqûm “to take” with -ma. ŠA.GA bīt abim mitḫāriš izuzzū is the phrase of §165–166: “the property of the father’s house they shall divide equally”.

sentences.l: If a-man for his-son to-uproot-(him) his-face has-set, to the-judges “my-son I-will-uproot” has-said,
sentences.i: If a man has set his face to cast out his son, and has said to the judges, “I will cast out my son,”
sentences.n: Disowning a son needs the judges. ana mārišu nasāḫim panam ištakan: panam šakānum “to set the face” is the idiom for making up one’s mind (§141); nasāḫim is the infinitive of nasāḫum “to uproot, pull out” (Harper: “to cut off, to disinherit”), so the object is to cast the son out of the family. ana dajjānī mārī anassaḫ iqtabi is “to the judges, ‘my son I shall cast out’, he has said”: mārī “my son” (DUMU and i), anassaḫ the first person present. Harper prints the numeral of XXVIII 14 at the foot of one page and its words at the top of the next; the plate has them as one line.

sentences.l: the-judges his-case they-shall-investigate-and,
sentences.i: the judges shall investigate his case, and
sentences.n: The judges do not simply grant it. warkassu is warkatum “the circumstances, the facts behind” + -šu “his” (the t and š merged): “his case”, as in §18. iparrasūma is the present plural of parāsum “to decide, to separate out, to investigate” (Harper: “to decide, to investigate, to inquire into”) with -ma.

sentences.l: if the-son a-grave offence which for sonship for-uprooting not he-has-brought, the-father his-son from sonship not he-shall-uproot.
sentences.i: if the son has not committed a grave offence of the kind that calls for casting him out of sonship, the father shall not cast his son out of sonship.
sentences.n: The rule: no cause, no disowning. arnam kabtam is “a heavy offence” (arnum “guilt, penalty”, kabtum “heavy”, accusative). ša ina ablūtim nasāḫim is “which, for uprooting from sonship”: ablūtum “sonship” is Harper’s word (from ablum, “son”), and nasāḫim the infinitive; lā ublam is “he has not brought” (wabālum with the ventive -am, “brought on himself”). The ruling is abum mārišu ina ablūtim ul inassaḫ, “the father shall not uproot his son from sonship”: inassaḫ is the third person present, where §168’s opening had the first person anassaḫ.

sentences.l: If a-grave offence which for sonship for-uprooting against his-father he-has-brought, for-the-first-time his-face they-shall-carry.
sentences.i: If he has committed against his father a grave offence calling for his being cast out of sonship, they shall overlook it (?) the first time.
sentences.n: The subject, the son, is not repeated. arnam kabtam ša ina ablūtim nasāḫim is the same clause as §168, now with ana abišu itbalam “he has brought (it) to his father”: itbalam is the preterite of tabālum “to carry off” with the ventive -am, as itbal at §45 (the perfect of wabālum would be ittabal), the verb that serves here for “bring on”. ana ištiššu is “for the first time”: ištiššu is ištēn “one” + -šu, in Harper’s glossary. panīšu ubbalū is “they shall carry his face”, ubbalū being the present plural of wabālum; “to carry the face” is an idiom for overlooking an offence, UNCERTAIN, and Harper’s “condone” is my guide for “overlook”.

sentences.l: If a-grave offence up-to his-second-time he-has-brought, the-father his-son from sonship he-shall-uproot.
sentences.i: If he has committed a grave offence a second time, the father shall cast his son out of sonship.
sentences.n: Only on the second offence may the father disown him. adi šinīšu is “up to his second” = “a second time” (adi “up to”, šinā “two”, -šu; Harper’s glossary lists šinīšu), like adi 10-šu “tenfold” in §8. inassaḫ is “he shall uproot”, now without ul “not”: the same sentence as §168, made positive. With it the stele leaves the family of sons and fathers; §170 begins with a man’s children by a wife and by a slave-woman.
